p: Fisher's Latin has Tampius; the older English splits it as "T. Ampius."
why: The lead's alignment chose the Latin form of the name for all five parts. The English reads the first letter as an abbreviation of a first name.

a: faithful to any trust given them
t: A damaged word in the Latin
p: The Latin text has a corrupt word here; the translation follows the sense of the older English.

readings.orig: their nation was more faithful than the other to any trust reposed in them
readings.en: their nation was more faithful than the other to any trust reposed in them
readings.plain: faithful to any trust given them

readings.orig: gens fidei patientior (the word between daggers, commissior, left out)
readings.en: a people more enduring in their loyalty (the daggered word left out, the rest translated word for word)

why: The editor of the Oxford text marks the word commissior with daggers as corrupt: gens fidei †commissior† patientior. The Conversational English Translation follows the sense of the Church and Brodribb English. The second reading here is not a manuscript reading: it is the Latin with the daggered word dropped and the rest translated. No manuscript is named for it.

p: The Latin spells the procurator's name differently from the older English.
why: Spelling-only differences keep the Church and Brodribb form (the lead's alignment rule). The Latin spelling is given here so the reader can see it.

p: The Latin has the 13th Gemina; the older English says the eighteenth.
why: The Latin words are tertia decima Gemina, the 13th Gemina. That is the legion that wintered at Petovio (3:1) and storms the Brixian gate at Cremona (3:27), so the older English "eighteenth" does not match the Latin or the rest of the book. The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin.

p: The Latin has the 1st and the 14th legions, the older English the first and the twelfth.

readings.en: the men of the 1st and the 14th

why: The Latin words are primani and quartadecimani, the men of the 1st and the 14th legions. The Church and Brodribb English has "twelfth," which does not match the Latin as printed by Fisher. The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin.

p: The Latin word means people who are not soldiers; the older English says "clowns."
why: The Latin word is pagani, civilians. The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin.

a: killed and stripped their relatives, in-laws and brothers
t: Killed and stripped, or stripped the bodies?
p: The Latin has two verbs, killed and stripped. The older English has only the stripping.

readings.en: they butcher and strip kinsmen, in-laws and brothers
readings.plain: killed and stripped their relatives, in-laws and brothers

readings.orig: stripped the bodies of slaughtered kinsfolk
readings.en: stripped the bodies of slaughtered kinsfolk
readings.plain: stripped the bodies of slaughtered kinsfolk

why: The Latin has trucidant spoliant, "they butcher, they strip." The Conversational English Translation keeps both verbs, so the soldiers kill their own kin in this war, not only rob the dead.

p: The Latin names the coverings and fillets of suppliants; the older English says olive branches and chaplets.

readings.orig: the olive-branches and chaplets of suppliants

why: The Latin words are velamenta et infulas. The Conversational English Translation names the wool bands and leaves the branches general.

t: Close to a massacre, or just beginning one?
p: The Latin says they were not far from slaughter; the older English says a massacre was just beginning.

readings.en: they were not far from slaughter

readings.orig: who were just beginning a massacre
readings.plain: at the start of a massacre

why: The Latin has nec procul caede aberant, "they were not far from slaughter." The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin.

p: The Latin abbreviates the second consul as P. Cornelius. The older English says Cornelius Scipio.

readings.en: in the consulship of Ti. Sempronius and P. Cornelius

why: The Latin gives the letters P. Cornelio and no more. The translation gives only what the Latin says.

p: The Latin has Publilius; the older English has Publius.
why: The lead's alignment chose the Latin name form.

a: men who fear danger and don't care about disgrace
t: Fearful of danger, or fond of it?
p: The Latin says the soldiers fear danger and care nothing for disgrace; the older English says they loved danger.

readings.en: fearful of dangers and unconcerned about disgrace
readings.plain: men who fear danger and don't care about disgrace

readings.orig: men who loved danger and were careless of disgrace
readings.en: men who loved danger and were careless of disgrace
readings.plain: men who loved danger and were careless of disgrace

why: The Latin word pavidos is "fearful," not "loving." The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin.

p: The Latin says Dacia was settled; the older English says Asia was calmed.

readings.orig: who in the meanwhile have reduced Asia to tranquillity

why: The Latin has Daciam, and the matter fits the context: Mucianus had sent the 6th legion against the Dacians (3:46). The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin.

t: Tore the empire, or mutilated its resources?
p: The Latin says he tore the empire itself; the older English narrows it to its resources.

readings.en: to tear the empire to pieces

readings.orig: he mutilated the resources of the Empire
readings.en: mutilated the resources of the Empire
readings.plain: mutilated the resources of the empire

why: The Latin object is imperium, the empire, not its resources.

p: The Latin says he was too much given to talk. The older English says he was somewhat boastful.

readings.en: he was too much given to talk

why: The Latin phrase sermonis nimius is about talk, not boasting.

p: The Latin has Vergilius; the older English has Verginius.
why: The lead's alignment chose the Latin name form.

p: The Latin names the captured cavalry prefect Julius Flavianus; the older English has Tullius.
why: The lead's alignment chose the Latin name form.

p: The Latin as printed has no verb and no word for "native place"; the older English supplies the sense.

readings.en: no verb: "father" and "Luceria", both in the accusative, with "to him"

why: The Latin as printed gives patrem ("father") and Luceriam ("Luceria") with illi ("to him") and no verb. Church and Brodribb's English says "Luceria was his native place," a sense the printed words do not state. The Conversational English Translation keeps the English sense; the site gives no repair of the Latin.

p: Tacitus and Suetonius count his 57th year; the epitome of Dio says 54 years and 89 days, which fits Suetonius's own birth date.

readings.w: Tacitus, Histories 3:86 (Fisher's Latin); Suetonius, Vitellius 18 (Thayer's page)
readings.orig: septimum et quinquagensimum aetatis annum explebat

readings.w: Cassius Dio, Epitome of book 64 (Thayer's page, section 22)
readings.orig: not seen in Greek; English only: fifty-four years and eighty-nine days

why: The Conversational English Translation translates Tacitus. Suetonius gives the same count (Vitellius 18), but his own birth date (the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Drusus Caesar and Norbanus Flaccus, Vitellius 3; Wikipedia dates it 24 September AD 15) makes Vitellius 54 when he died in December 69, as Dio's epitome says. The 57th-year count in both Latin writers does not fit it. Church and Brodribb have "nearly completed" for the Latin explebat.
